title: Weaving in ends
subtitle: Securing yarn tails so they stay hidden without adding bulk.
excerpt: Weaving in ends secures the loose yarn tails left at cast-on, cast-off, and colour changes by threading them through the fabric with the tapestry needle. A well-woven end stays invisible and holds through washing, wear, and blocking.
sourceNotes: Standard finishing technique common to all UK and US knitting traditions. Weldon's Practical Knitter finishing notes describe securing ends by darning. Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938) details the weave-under-bar method.
heroPrompt: A tapestry needle weaving a yarn tail through the purl bumps on the wrong side of a knitted swatch, the tail nearly invisible against the fabric.

glossaryTerms.definition: The loose end of yarn left at the start or finish of a piece, or at a colour change, which must be secured before the item is worn or washed.

content.text: Every knitted piece has at least two

(cast-on and cast-off), and more at every colour change. Weaving these tails through the wrong side of the fabric secures them so they do not unravel in use. The method described here works on stocking stitch, garter stitch, and ribbing; the same principle applies to any knitted fabric. Difficulty: beginner.
A blunt tapestry needle with an eye large enough for your yarn
Thread the yarn tail onto the tapestry needle. Turn the piece to the wrong side.
On stocking stitch, weave the needle diagonally under the horizontal bars (the purl bumps on the wrong side) for about 4-5 stitches in one direction.
Turn and weave back in the opposite direction for another 3-4 stitches, going slightly up or down a row. This reversal locks the tail in place.
Pull the fabric gently in all directions to check the tail does not show on the right side.
Trim the tail close to the fabric, leaving about 3 mm. Do not trim flush with the fabric, as this risks the end working its way through after washing.

attrs.title: Weaving in ribbing and garter stitch
attrs.body: On ribbing, follow the path of a single column of stitches rather than weaving across rows. This hides the tail inside the rib structure. On garter stitch, weave under the ridge loops on the wrong side, alternating direction as above.

content.text: Every finished knitted piece requires weaving in ends. Colour-work garments may have dozens of tails to secure. The technique is always the last step before blocking, as blocking can shift the woven tails slightly and reveal them if they have not been woven in securely.

items.symptom: The tail shows through on the right side
items.cause: The needle caught both layers of the stitch rather than just the bar on the wrong side
items.fix: Weave only under the surface bars and purl bumps on the wrong side. Check as you go by turning the work over after every few stitches.

items.symptom: The tail works loose after washing
items.cause: Too short a length was woven, or the direction reversal was skipped
items.fix: Weave at least 4-5 stitches in each direction, always reversing course at least once. Superwash wool and plant fibres need longer weaving runs because the yarns are smoother and tails slip more easily.

items.symptom: The yarn splits or shreds while being threaded
items.cause: The tapestry needle is too sharp, or the eye is too small
items.fix: Use a blunt needle with an eye wide enough for the yarn to pass through without compression. Threading from the folded end of the yarn rather than the cut end reduces splitting.
